newsitem.title: GERMANY: German post offices close early as protest widens.
newsitem.headline: German post offices close early as protest widens.

text.p: Post office counters in 52 German towns closed early on Saturday as 8,000 postal workers staged fresh work stoppages against a new draft law that would remove the German post office's monopoly, the postal trade union said.

The Deutsche Postgewerkschaft (DPG) union said around 1,500 counter staff stopped work at 10 a.m., while a further 6,500 post delivery workers also joined the protest, which was particularly strong in the cities of Berlin and Hamburg.

The action comes as speculation mounts that the German postal market is to be freed up to competition earlier and more completely than previously expected because of pressure from some politicians within the Bonn coalition.
"If the Bonn government puts through its plans..., people will end up with a poorer, scaled-down, and more expensive postal service," the DPG said in a statement.
The Bonn government is due on Tuesday to discuss the new draft law, which would sweep aside the post office's century-old monopoly.

Pressure from free-market advocates within the junior coalition party, the Free Democrats (FDP), is widely expected to ensure that earlier plans to grant the post office a five-year exclusive operator licence will not be approved.

Moreover, the part of the market reserved for the existing Post AG post office, which is eventually to be privatised, is thought likely to be limited to letters up to 100 grams in weight, and not the 350 grams initially envisaged.
Post AG managing director Klaus Zumwinkel, in an interview due to be published on Sunday, described the FDP's push to throw the postal market open to free competition as "nonsensical".

"We need an exclusive licence to be able to finance legally binding commitments that we have, for example in the area of pension payments," Zumwinkel was quoted as saying in a summary of an interview in Sunday's Welt am Sonntag.
"The FDP has for political reasons determined that we must bear these billion-mark costs and wants now to stop the post office from being able to finance such costs," he added.

The DPG also fears the new postal law would open up the market to "cherry-picking", in which rival operators would be able to operate in the most lucrative parts of the market, ignoring the least attractive market segments.
It said such a move could put tens of thousands of existing post office jobs at risk.
The union plans a mass demonstration against the law involving some 10,000 people in Bonn on Monday.
